lessonRef.unitTitle: Paragraph Power: Informative and Explanatory Writing
lessonRef.focus: writing a short explainer on an unfamiliar topic from given facts
lessonRef.title: Transfer to a new text: writing a short explainer on an unfamiliar topic from given facts

studentTask.text: This Grade 3 lesson develops writing a short explainer on an unfamiliar topic from given facts within the unit “Paragraph Power: Informative and Explanatory Writing.” Read the delivered Academy-original source before responding. Strong ELA work separates what the source explicitly says from what a reader infers, selects evidence because it is relevant and sufficient, and explains the connection instead of leaving a quotation to speak for itself. Today's transfer to a new text work asks you to make that reasoning visible and to revise if the evidence does not support the first idea.

sourceReference.text:
A honeybee that finds a good patch of flowers faces a problem. The patch may be far from the hive, and the bee cannot lead thousands of other bees there one at a time. Instead, it dances.

Back inside the dark hive, the returning bee moves across the honeycomb in a repeating pattern. Other bees crowd close and follow the movement with their antennae. The dance carries real information.

The direction of the dance tells the other bees which way to fly. Because the hive is dark and vertical, the bee cannot simply point at the sun. Instead, straight up on the honeycomb stands for the direction of the sun. If the flowers are forty degrees to the right of the sun, the dancing bee angles forty degrees to the right of straight up.

The length of the dance tells the other bees how far to fly. A longer run means a longer trip. A very short dance, done in tight circles, usually means the food is close to home.

The energy of the dance carries a third message. A bee that has found an excellent patch dances harder and repeats the pattern more times. A weaker patch produces a shorter, calmer dance, and fewer bees are convinced to go.

The result is a hive that sends most of its workers to the best food available, without any single bee being in charge of the decision.

guidedSupport.text:
Use this source-specific routine for “Why Bees Dance”:
1. Preview the title and paragraph structure; write what writing a short explainer on an unfamiliar topic from given facts asks you to notice or do.
2. Mark one statement the source makes explicitly and one inference a reader could draw. Keep the two kinds of thinking separate.
3. Test the inference with the evidence requirement in today's task. If the evidence is weak or incomplete, narrow or revise the inference.
4. Draft your own response. A facilitator may clarify directions or ask questions, but may not supply your claim, evidence choice, sentences, or revision.

independentEvidenceTask.text:
Read “Why Bees Dance,” then answer: Transfer writing a short explainer on an unfamiliar topic from given facts to a different paragraph or perspective in the reading. What had to change in your approach?

Deliverable: Grade 3: a transfer response and a precise explanation of the adjustment; write 3–5 complete sentences.

Evidence requirement: Use one exact detail. Label source evidence with a paragraph number or another precise location. Your response must explain the connection between the evidence and your conclusion.

remediation.text:
If writing a short explainer on an unfamiliar topic from given facts is not yet secure, return to “Why Bees Dance” before starting over:
- Evidence gap: underline the exact words that support the idea and label their paragraph or location.
- Reasoning gap: complete the stem “This evidence matters because …” in your own words, then reread the question.
- Overclaim: name what the source does not establish and narrow the conclusion to what the evidence can support.
- Completion gap: compare the draft with each learner success criterion and repair one missing part at a time.

extension.text: Apply writing a short explainer on an unfamiliar topic from given facts to a different paragraph or a defensible alternative interpretation of “Why Bees Dance.” Compare the new result with your first response and explain which evidence changes, which reasoning still holds, and why.
